The invention relates to systems and methods for storing spent nuclear fuel in a below-grade configuration while still maintaining adequate ventilation of the storage cavity. In general, the system is designed to receive and store a spent nuclear fuel canister at least partially beneath ground level, thereby providing shielding, protection, and efficient use of space, while also allowing heat generated by the spent fuel to be removed through passive or assisted air circulation.

The system includes a shell that defines an internal cavity sized and shaped to receive a spent nuclear fuel canister. At least a portion of the shell is positioned below grade when the system is installed. The shell may be formed from metal, concrete, composite materials, or combinations of materials suitable for structural support, radiation shielding, corrosion resistance, and long-term durability. The cavity formed by the shell provides a storage region into which the spent nuclear fuel canister may be lowered and supported during use.

To ventilate the cavity, the system includes at least one inlet ventilation duct. The inlet ventilation duct extends from an inlet located above grade to an outlet located below grade, preferably near a lower portion or bottom region of the cavity. In this arrangement, air can enter the system from above ground, travel downwardly through the ventilation duct, and be discharged near the bottom of the cavity. The air may then flow upwardly through or around the cavity, absorbing heat from the spent nuclear fuel canister, before exiting through one or more outlet vents or exhaust pathways. This ventilation arrangement helps maintain the canister and surrounding storage structure within acceptable temperature limits.

The ventilation duct is connected to the shell in a manner that preserves the integrity of the storage cavity. In particular, the connection between the duct and the shell is configured so that the cavity is hermetically sealed against ingress of below-grade fluids. As a result, groundwater, stormwater, or other subsurface fluids are prevented from entering the cavity through the duct-to-shell interface or through other below-grade portions of the system. This sealing feature is especially important for long-term storage installations, where exposure to moisture or chemically aggressive fluids could affect the performance or durability of the storage components.

The invention also includes methods of installing and using the system. In one method, a hole is formed below grade at a selected storage site. The shell and associated ventilation components are placed into the hole so that at least part of the shell is located below ground level while the ventilation inlet remains above grade. After the system is positioned, the hole is filled with engineered fill. The engineered fill may be selected and compacted to provide structural support, drainage control, thermal performance, and stability around the below-grade storage system.

Once the system has been installed, a spent nuclear fuel canister is lowered into the cavity formed by the shell. The canister may be inserted using a crane, hoist, transfer cask, or other suitable handling equipment. After placement, the ventilation duct provides an airflow path from the above-grade inlet to the lower region of the cavity, enabling air circulation that removes decay heat from the stored canister. In this manner, the system provides below-grade storage of spent nuclear fuel while maintaining ventilation and protecting the cavity from intrusion by below-grade fluids.
outputs.L4:
The system and method relate to the below-grade storage of spent nuclear fuel in a manner that provides both passive cooling and environmental protection. In general, the system includes a storage shell or liner positioned within a cavity formed below ground level. The cavity is sized and configured to receive a spent nuclear fuel canister, such as a sealed dry storage canister, so that the canister is stored substantially underground rather than in a fully exposed above-grade installation.

A ventilation arrangement is provided to remove decay heat generated by the spent fuel. The ventilation path includes one or more ducts extending between an above-grade location and the below-grade shell cavity. Air may enter and exit through these ducts by natural convection, forced flow, or a combination of both. As the canister gives off heat, air circulating through the ventilation path absorbs the heat and carries it away from the storage cavity, thereby maintaining the canister within acceptable thermal limits.

An important feature of the system is that the ventilation ducting is arranged to preserve hermetic sealing of the below-grade storage region against groundwater, stormwater, soil moisture, or other below-grade fluids. The duct may be sealed, isolated, elevated, routed, or otherwise configured so that air can move between the underground cavity and the outside environment without creating a direct fluid intrusion pathway into the storage shell. In this way, the system permits ventilation while reducing the risk that water or other subsurface fluids will enter the storage cavity and contact the canister or associated structural components.

The storage shell can provide physical protection for the canister, shielding it from external impacts, weather, and certain environmental hazards. Because the canister is placed below grade, the surrounding earth can also contribute to shielding and structural protection. At the same time, the above-grade-to-below-grade ventilation system allows heat to be dissipated without requiring the canister to be exposed above ground.

The method of use generally includes forming a below-grade cavity, installing a storage shell or liner within the cavity, providing a sealed ventilation duct arrangement between the below-grade cavity and an above-grade air inlet or outlet, and placing a spent nuclear fuel canister into the shell. Once installed, the system allows air circulation for cooling while maintaining isolation from below-grade fluids. The result is a protected underground storage configuration that improves thermal management, enhances isolation of the spent fuel canister, and reduces the likelihood of fluid ingress into the storage environment.

Systems are all around us. A system is a group of connected parts that work together to achieve a purpose or produce a result. These parts can be physical, digital, social, or natural. For example, the human body is a biological system, a computer is a technological system, a company is an organizational system, and the climate is a natural system.

One important feature of systems is that each part affects the others. In a transportation system, roads, vehicles, traffic lights, drivers, and rules all interact. If one part changes, such as a road closure or an increase in traffic, the whole system may be affected. This is why understanding systems requires looking not only at individual parts but also at the relationships between them.

Systems can be simple or complex. A simple system, like a lamp, has only a few parts and is easy to understand. A complex system, like the internet or a city, includes many parts that interact in unpredictable ways. In complex systems, small changes can sometimes create large effects.

Studying systems helps people solve problems more effectively. Instead of focusing only on one issue, systems thinking encourages us to look at causes, connections, patterns, and long-term consequences. This approach is useful in science, business, engineering, education, healthcare, and environmental planning.

In the modern world, systems are becoming increasingly interconnected. Digital systems connect people across the globe, economic systems influence markets and jobs, and environmental systems affect life on Earth. Understanding how systems work is essential for making better decisions and creating solutions that are efficient, sustainable, and adaptable.

counterfactuals.output: An underground spent nuclear fuel storage system includes a below-grade storage cavity configured to receive one or more sealed fuel canisters and a closure structure arranged to substantially isolate the cavity from the surrounding environment. The storage cavity is formed within an engineered vault or bore and includes radiation-shielding sidewalls, a base support, and a removable or permanent upper seal. One or more ventilation ducts extend between the storage cavity and an above-grade or near-grade air interface to permit passive or assisted circulation of cooling air along a heat-transfer path thermally coupled to the stored canisters while maintaining physical separation between the cooling airflow and the sealed cavity interior. The ducts may include inlet and outlet passages arranged to promote natural convection, filtration, flow control, and environmental protection. counterfactuals.prompt: Describe systems and methods for storing spent nuclear fuel canisters underground while maintaining airflow and preventing ingress of below-grade fluids.
counterfactuals.output:
Systems and methods for underground storage of spent nuclear fuel canisters can combine a below-grade structural storage cavity with passive ventilation pathways and engineered barriers that prevent groundwater, stormwater, and other below-grade fluids from entering the canister storage region.

## System Description

An underground spent fuel storage system may include:

1. **Below-grade storage vault or cavity**
   - A reinforced concrete or steel-lined underground vault, borehole, caisson, or module.
   - The vault receives one or more sealed spent nuclear fuel canisters, such as dry storage canisters containing fuel assemblies.
   - The canister is positioned within an overpack or support structure that maintains spacing between the canister exterior and the surrounding vault wall.

2. **Canister support and alignment structure**
   - Internal rails, cradles, pedestals, spacers, or centering guides support the canister.
   - These components define an annular airflow passage around the canister.
   - The support structure may elevate the canister above the vault floor to prevent contact with any incidental liquid and to allow air circulation beneath the canister.

3. **Passive airflow circuit**
   - One or more air inlet ducts communicate between the atmosphere and a lower portion of the underground vault.
   - One or more air outlet ducts communicate between an upper portion of the vault and the atmosphere.
   - Decay heat from the spent fuel warms air in the annular space around the canister, producing natural convection.
   - Cooler air enters through lower inlets, flows upward around the canister, removes heat, and exits through upper outlets.

4. **Above-grade vent terminations**
   - Air inlet and outlet openings may terminate above expected flood levels.
   - Vent risers can include weather hoods, louvers, screens, debris guards, and radiation shielding bends.
   - Vent paths may include tortuous sections to reduce streaming radiation while preserving airflow.

5. **Fluid-ingress prevention barriers**
   - The vault may include exterior waterproofing membranes, bentonite layers, sealants, coatings, or corrosion-resistant liners.
   - Joints, penetrations, and seams may be sealed with waterstops, gaskets, welded sleeves, or compression seals.
   - Vent ducts may be sloped, trapped, baffled, or provided with drains to prevent rainwater or floodwater from flowing into the storage cavity.

6. **Drainage and fluid management**
   - A perimeter drainage system may surround the underground module.
   - Drain pipes, gravel packs, geotextiles, and sump structures can direct groundwater away from the vault.
   - Any incidental water entering non-storage portions of the system can be collected in a sump separated from the canister cavity.
   - Check valves, backflow preventers, or passive flap valves may prevent reverse flow into ventilation ducts or drains.

7. **Isolation of airflow from groundwater paths**
   - Ventilation ducts are isolated from soil and groundwater by sealed conduit walls.
   - Penetrations through the vault wall are sealed using embedded sleeves and redundant gaskets or welds.
   - The air path remains open to the atmosphere while being physically separated from below-grade fluid pathways.

8. **Removable closure or access plug**
   - The upper end of the vault may include a shield plug, closure lid, hatch, or removable cover.
   - The closure can provide structural shielding while allowing defined airflow passages.
   - Seals between the closure and vault body prevent surface water from entering the storage cavity.

9. **Monitoring and inspection features**
   - Temperature sensors may monitor canister surface temperature, outlet air temperature, or vault air temperature.
   - Humidity or liquid detection sensors may detect abnormal moisture ingress.
   - Airflow sensors or differential pressure sensors may verify ventilation performance.
   - Sampling ports may permit periodic inspection of air quality or contamination levels.

## Example Method of Operation

A representative method for storing spent nuclear fuel underground may include:

1. **Providing a sealed spent fuel canister**
   - Spent fuel assemblies are loaded into a certified dry storage canister.
   - The canister is dried, backfilled with inert gas if required, and sealed.

2. **Preparing the underground storage module**
   - A below-grade vault or borehole is constructed with structural reinforcement and waterproofing.
   - Air inlet and outlet ducts are installed so that their openings terminate above grade.
   - Drainage systems are installed around or beneath the vault to reduce hydrostatic pressure.

3. **Installing the canister**
   - The sealed canister is lowered into the underground vault.
   - The canister is supported on pedestals, rails, or centering devices to preserve airflow gaps.
   - A closure plug or lid is installed while maintaining communication with ventilation passages.

4. **Establishing passive cooling airflow**
   - Ambient air enters through one or more lower inlet ducts.
   - The air flows upward around the canister due to heat-driven buoyancy.
   - Heated air exits through upper outlet ducts.
   - The airflow path is maintained without powered fans, although auxiliary fans may be provided for testing or abnormal conditions.

5. **Preventing ingress of below-grade fluids**
   - Exterior waterproofing, sealed joints, and lined penetrations prevent groundwater intrusion.
   - Perimeter drains lower local water pressure around the vault.
   - Vent risers are elevated and shaped to prevent rainwater entry.
   - Backflow devices and drain traps prevent water from traveling through ducts into the vault.
   - Any incidental liquid is routed away from the canister region or collected in a monitored sump.

6. **Monitoring storage conditions**
   - Temperatures are monitored to confirm adequate decay heat removal.
   - Moisture sensors verify that the cavity remains dry.
   - Airflow or pressure measurements confirm that inlet and outlet paths remain unobstructed.
   - Periodic inspections verify the integrity of vents, seals, drains, and structural components.

## Design Variations

The system may be implemented in several configurations, including:

- **Single-canister vertical borehole storage**, where each canister is placed in an individual lined shaft.
- **Horizontal underground storage modules**, where canisters are inserted into laterally extending tunnels or vaults.
- **Multi-canister vaults**, where several canisters are stored in separate sleeves sharing a common ventilation plenum.
- **Hybrid passive/active ventilation systems**, where natural convection is primary and powered ventilation is available as backup.
- **Double-wall vault systems**, where an inner dry storage cavity is surrounded by an outer drainage or inspection annulus.

## Key Functional Features

Such a system maintains safety by combining:

- sealed dry canisters for radioactive material confinement;
- underground shielding and physical protection;
- passive convective airflow for decay heat removal;
- elevated and protected air vents to preserve ventilation;
- waterproof structural barriers and drainage to prevent groundwater ingress;
- monitoring systems to detect abnormal temperature, moisture, or airflow conditions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft the “summary of the invention” section for a nuclear spent fuel storage system comprising a shell, a below-grade cavity, above-grade ventilation inlet, engineered fill, and canister lowering method.
counterfactuals.output:
## Summary of the Invention

The present invention provides a system and method for storing nuclear spent fuel in a below-grade storage configuration that provides passive thermal management, structural protection, and controlled installation of a spent fuel canister. In one embodiment, the system includes a shell disposed within a below-grade cavity formed in the earth, the shell defining an interior receiving space configured to receive a spent fuel canister. The shell may be formed from metal, concrete, composite materials, or combinations thereof, and may be configured to maintain a separation between the canister and surrounding soil or engineered fill.

In certain embodiments, the below-grade cavity is excavated to a depth sufficient to position at least a substantial portion of the spent fuel canister below an adjacent grade level. The cavity may be lined, reinforced, or otherwise prepared to receive the shell. An engineered fill material may be disposed between an exterior surface of the shell and the surrounding cavity wall. The engineered fill may provide one or more of structural support, drainage, radiation shielding, seismic load distribution, thermal conduction, and long-term stabilization of the storage installation. In some embodiments, the engineered fill comprises granular material, concrete, grout, thermally conductive backfill, low-permeability material, or layered combinations thereof.

The system further includes a ventilation arrangement configured to promote passive cooling of the spent fuel canister. In one embodiment, at least one ventilation inlet is positioned above grade and is in fluid communication with a lower portion of the shell or cavity. Air entering the above-grade ventilation inlet may flow downwardly and/or laterally into the storage structure and then pass along or around the canister to remove decay heat by natural convection. Heated air may be discharged through one or more outlet passages, vents, stacks, or ducts. In particular embodiments, the above-grade ventilation inlet is configured to reduce water intrusion, debris ingress, flooding effects, or blockage while permitting sufficient airflow for passive heat removal.

In another embodiment, the shell includes one or more flow passages, annular channels, spacers, stand-offs, or internal supports arranged to maintain airflow around the spent fuel canister. The shell may be configured to support the canister in a generally vertical orientation within the below-grade cavity while providing a cooling air pathway between the canister and the shell. The system may further include shielding structures, closure assemblies, access covers, impact-resistant components, or security features located at or near grade level.

The invention also provides a method for installing a spent fuel canister in a below-grade storage system. In one embodiment, the method includes forming a below-grade cavity, positioning a shell within the cavity, placing engineered fill around at least a portion of the shell, and establishing an above-grade ventilation inlet in fluid communication with the shell. The method further includes lowering a spent fuel canister into the shell. The canister may be lowered using a crane, hoist, transfer cask, guided frame, alignment fixture, or other lifting apparatus. During lowering, the canister may be guided into the shell to prevent excessive lateral movement, impact, or misalignment.

In certain embodiments, the canister lowering method includes positioning a transfer cask above the shell, aligning the transfer cask with an opening of the shell, and lowering the canister from the transfer cask into the shell while maintaining shielding around the canister. After the canister is received within the shell, a closure, cover, lid, shield plug, or ventilation cap may be installed. The ventilation inlet and associated airflow paths may remain open to provide passive cooling during storage.

The system and method described herein may provide improved protection of spent fuel canisters by placing the canister at least partially below grade, thereby reducing exposure to external hazards while maintaining passive heat removal through above-grade ventilation. The engineered fill may enhance stability and thermal performance, and the shell may provide a durable receiving structure for long-term storage. Various embodiments may be implemented as standalone storage modules or as part of an array of multiple below-grade storage installations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create patent claim-like language for an underground spent nuclear fuel storage system that uses a hermetically sealed shell and ventilation duct from above grade to near the cavity bottom.
counterfactuals.output:
1. An underground spent nuclear fuel storage system comprising:  
   an underground cavity formed below grade and configured to receive at least one spent nuclear fuel canister;  
   a shell disposed within the underground cavity, the shell defining an interior storage volume and being hermetically sealed to isolate the interior storage volume from surrounding geological media and groundwater;  
   a closure assembly coupled to an upper portion of the shell and configured to maintain a hermetic boundary of the shell; and  
   a ventilation duct extending from an inlet located above grade to an outlet positioned within the underground cavity proximate a bottom region of the shell,  
   wherein the ventilation duct is configured to deliver cooling air from above grade to the bottom region such that heat generated by the spent nuclear fuel canister promotes upward convective airflow along the shell.

2. The system of claim 1, wherein the shell comprises a corrosion-resistant metallic liner.

3. The system of claim 1, wherein the shell is formed as a continuous welded structure.

4. The system of claim 1, wherein the hermetically sealed shell prevents ingress of liquid water into the interior storage volume.

5. The system of claim 1, wherein the ventilation duct is external to the hermetically sealed interior storage volume.

6. The system of claim 1, wherein the ventilation duct terminates adjacent a lower end of the underground cavity to establish a chimney-effect cooling path extending upwardly from the outlet toward an above-grade exhaust region.

7. The system of claim 1, further comprising an annular flow passage between the shell and a surrounding wall of the underground cavity, the annular flow passage being in fluid communication with the ventilation duct outlet.

8. The system of claim 7, wherein the annular flow passage is configured to conduct heated air upwardly to an exhaust vent above grade.

9. The system of claim 1, further comprising a support structure within the hermetically sealed shell configured to support the spent nuclear fuel canister in a substantially vertical orientation.

10. The system of claim 1, wherein the closure assembly includes a seal weld.

11. The system of claim 1, wherein the closure assembly includes at least one monitored seal configured to indicate loss of hermetic integrity.

12. The system of claim 1, wherein the ventilation duct is configured to provide passive cooling without an electrically powered fan.

13. The system of claim 1, wherein the above-grade inlet includes a weather hood and a radiation shield structure.

14. The system of claim 1, wherein the underground cavity comprises a borehole, shaft, vault, or silo.

15. The system of claim 1, wherein the shell includes a cylindrical sidewall and a closed lower end.

16. The system of claim 1, wherein the ventilation duct extends downwardly along an exterior side of the shell.

17. The system of claim 1, wherein the ventilation duct extends through a backfill or grout region surrounding the shell.

18. The system of claim 1, wherein the ventilation duct outlet is located below a lower end of the spent nuclear fuel canister when the spent nuclear fuel canister is positioned within the shell.

19. The system of claim 1, further comprising a radiation shielding plug positioned above the spent nuclear fuel canister and below grade.

20. A method of cooling spent nuclear fuel stored underground, the method comprising:  
   placing a spent nuclear fuel canister within an interior storage volume of a shell disposed in an underground cavity;  
   hermetically sealing the shell to isolate the spent nuclear fuel canister from groundwater and surrounding geological media;  
   admitting ambient air into a ventilation duct through an inlet located above grade;  
   conveying the ambient air downward through the ventilation duct to an outlet positioned proximate a bottom region of the underground cavity; and  
   transferring heat from the spent nuclear fuel canister through the hermetically sealed shell to the air, thereby inducing upward convective flow from the bottom region toward an exhaust region above grade.
